IQWiG also demands robust data on safety, patient‑reported outcomes, and health‑economic impact.  Importantly, Germany is moving toward a “value‑based” reimbursement model for digital therapeutics; therefore, evidence of downstream cost savings (e.g., reduced smoking‑related morbidity) or improved quality of life that can be quantified in QALYs will be critical.

In both the UK and Germany a prescription digital therapeutic (PDT) must first obtain regulatory clearance as a medical device before it can be marketed or prescribed. In the UK this is achieved through the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA). The MHRA classifies PDTs under the Medical Devices Regulations 2002, amended by the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR 2017/745) until the end of the transition period in December 2023, after which the UK‑specific Medical Devices Regulations 2021 apply. A Class IIa or higher device requires a conformity assessment by an approved notified body and a CE‑UK mark; for a prescription‑only product, the manufacturer must also register with the MHRA’s Digital Health Innovation Hub (DHIH) and obtain a “Medical Device Licence” under the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2021. The MHRA’s guidance on “Digital Therapeutics: Guidance for Developers” (latest version 2023) sets out the evidence requirements, risk‑management, clinical evaluation, and post‑market surveillance obligations that must be satisfied within an 18‑month launch window.

In Germany a PDT is regulated by the Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices (BfArM). The device falls under the German Medicines Act (AMG) and the German Medical Device Regulation (in force since 2023), which incorporates the MDR. Approval requires a “CE‑UK” mark if the product was first approved in the UK, or a German CE‑Mark if it is being introduced directly into Germany. The BfArM’s “Regulation on the approval of medical devices for use as digital health applications” (BfArM‑Verordnung) mandates that the manufacturer submit a technical file, clinical evidence, and a risk assessment. For prescription‑only PDTs, a “Katalogeintrag” in the BfArM catalogue is required before prescribing can commence. The German Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices also coordinates with the Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG) and the Federal Joint Committee (G‑BA) for health technology assessment (HTA), which will influence reimbursement decisions.

**Data protection obligations under GDPR, UK DPA 2018, and BDSG**

All three regimes impose a common set of data‑protection principles: lawfulness, fairness, transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality. The GDPR remains the overarching framework for cross‑border processing in both jurisdictions. Under Article 6(1)(f) or (1)(b), the PDT must identify a lawful basis—most likely legitimate interest or public interest in health, supplemented by explicit consent where necessary. The UK DPA 2018, while largely aligned with GDPR, introduces specific provisions on “special category data” for health and “data protection impact assessments” (DPIAs) that are mandatory when processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals’ rights. The BDSG supplements the GDPR by imposing stricter rules on employee data, data transfer to third parties, and the appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO).
